extracted.intended_audience: marketing researchers, content strategists, journalists, and academics studying online virality
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and empirical criteria for what makes online news (and related marketing) content more likely to be shared/viral, based on archival analysis and experiments testing specific emotions and content features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activation/arousal
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of activation (arousal) that content evokes drives social transmission: higher arousal increases sharing, lower (deactivating) emotions decrease sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured via activation index (e.g., scales anchored very passive/very active, very mellow/very fired up). Experimental mediation analyses show arousal mediates effects of specific emotions (amusement, anger, sadness) on sharing. Design implication: craft content that evokes activation (high arousal) to boost virality; avoid content that primarily evokes deactivating emotions like sadness if the goal is sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awe
rubrics_metrics.description: Awe is a high-arousal positive emotion that is positively linked to virality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-standard-deviation increase in awe increases the odds of making the most-e-mailed list by ~30% (Field results, Table 4, Model 4). Use awe-inspiring angles to increase sharing probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anxiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Anxiety, a high-arousal negative emotion, is positively associated with transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-standard-deviation increase in anxiety increases the odds of making the most-e-mailed list by ~21%. Anxiety-evoking content (e.g., anxiety-inducing ad scenarios) can increase sharing because of induced activation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Anger, another high-arousal negative emotion, strongly increases the likelihood content will be shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-standard-deviation increase in anger increases odds of making the most-e-mailed list by ~34%. Experimental manipulations (Study 2b: high-anger vs low-anger customer-service story) confirm causal impact via arousal mediation. Note brand risks: anger may increase transmission even if it hurts brand attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sadness (deactivating emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sadness, a low-arousal/deactivating negative emotion, reduces the likelihood of sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-standard-deviation increase in sadness decreases the odds of making the most-e-mailed list by ~16%. Experiments (Study 3) show high-sadness condition reduces arousal and sharing; thus evoking sadness can suppress transmission even if the story is compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valence / Positivity
rubrics_metrics.description: General positivity (positive valence) of content is positively related to sharing: more positive content is more viral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-standard-deviation increase in positivity increases odds of making the list by ~13%. However, valence alone is insufficient—arousal moderates effects (positive high-arousal emotions like awe/amusement drive sharing more).

rubrics_metrics.name: General emotionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall emotional content (emotionality) of an article increases likelihood of sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-standard-deviation increase in emotionality increases odds by ~18%. But the specific emotion matters (see awe/anger/anxiety vs sadness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: How interesting a story is (interest) positively predicts transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-standard-deviation increase in interest increases odds of making the list by ~25%. Pretests in experiments ensured manipulations did not differ on interest when isolating specific emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-standard-deviation increase in surprise increases odds by ~14%. Surprise may contribute to making content 'contagious' by making it more noteworthy to share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical value / Utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically useful content (useful information) increases the probability of being shared via e-mail but may differ by sharing channel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-standard-deviation increase in practical value increases odds of making the most-e-mailed list by ~30%. However, analysis shows practically useful stories are marginally less likely to be blogged about (possible explanation: blogs already provide commentary). Consider channel when emphasizing practical utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: External attention drivers (prominence/time on home page)
rubrics_metrics.description: External placement and prominent exposure (e.g., time as lead story on homepage) substantially increase sharing independent of content characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field estimates: a one-standard-deviation increase in time at top of home page increases odds by ~20% (equivalent to several extra hours as lead story). Compare magnitude with content effects; content characteristics are of similar importance. When feasible, secure prominent placement to amplify sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article metadata and controls (section, timing, location)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper location, web timing, article section (e.g., arts, books), and day fixed effects influence observed virality and should be controlled for in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regression models include day fixed effects and section dummies; models 4–6 include additional controls (e.g., disgust). When evaluating virality, account for publication timing and placement to avoid confounding content effects with exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author attributes (first-author fame, female first author, uncredited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Author-level characteristics were included as predictors (first-author fame, female first author indicator, uncredited) in regression analyses predicting being on the most-e-mailed list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characteristics may influence sharing; include author-level covariates when modeling virality to isolate content effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disgust (as a control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disgust was hand-coded and included as a control because prior research linked disgust to transmission; in these analyses its effect was never significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including disgust as a control provides a conservative test of emotion hypotheses; dropping it does not change key results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of sharing moderates effects (e-mail vs blogging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different sharing modes (narrowcasting via e-mail vs broadcasting via blogs/social networks) show similar drivers but with some differences (e.g., practical utility effects reverse for blogging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis of most-blogged lists suggests emotionality, positivity, interest, and anger increase blogging as well, while practical utility may reduce blogging. Consider intended sharing channel when designing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness and model specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Results should be checked across multiple model specifications and robustness checks (e.g., hand-coded subset, removing day fixed effects, alternate emotion quantification, alternate dependent measures like article rank or time on list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports findings are robust across many checks; practice: test effects on different subsets and with alternate operationalizations to ensure findings are not artifacts of model choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design implication for marketers: target arousal, not just valence
rubrics_metrics.description: When crafting contagious content (ads or articles), aim to evoke high-arousal emotions (amusement, awe, anger, anxiety) rather than low-arousal positive states (contentment) or sadness for greater sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: humorous ads (amusement) or anxiety-inducing short films (BMW 'The Hire') increased sharing; advertisers can intentionally evoke activating emotions to boost viral diffusion, but should weigh brand/ethical trade-offs of negative high-arousal content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sender internal states vs receiver-focused motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharing is influenced by the sender's internal emotional state as well as by recipient-oriented motives (helping, informing, reputation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should consider how content affects the sharer's internal states (activation) in addition to recipient value; empirical measures of sender activation can help predict sharing behavior.
